# George Native 0.1: algorithm and resource contract

This is an original, experimental C implementation, not a translation or fork of Bergman or Singular. The accompanying George overlay connects it to the existing form and results UI. It is not a replacement for all of George's computations.

## Mathematical scope

The coefficient field is Q (modulus=0), or an explicitly selected prime field F_p for p<=2147483647. In characteristic zero all stored polynomials are primitive integer representatives of rational polynomials. Dividing by integer content is correct over Q; this is NOT computation of a strong basis over Z. Exact internal coefficients promote from a signed 63-bit tagged immediate to arbitrary-length base-2^32 magnitudes. Input coefficients currently must fit the signed immediate range, -(2^62-1)..2^62-1. There is no floating-point arithmetic in an algebraic decision and no silent modular substitution.

There are 1..16 noncommuting generators, each of degree one. Input relations are homogeneous of positive degree. The order is degree followed by left lexicographic, with the LAST declared generator largest. Target degree is at most 20. Ideals are two-sided ideals of the free associative algebra. Modules, weighted orders, nonhomogeneous relations, commutative polynomial rings, Anick resolutions, and Poincare-Betti series are not supported by this backend.

A result `complete:true` means all required compositions THROUGH THE REQUESTED DEGREE have been processed. It never asserts that the unbounded Groebner basis is finite or complete. The output has primitive coefficients and a minimal set of leading words, but is NOT advertised as a fully reduced, canonical Groebner basis (`reduced:false`). Later rules can reduce tails of previously stored rules.

## Completion invariant

Degrees are processed in increasing order. Input relations of degree d are reduced and inserted before processing overlaps of total degree d. Every inserted rule is an exact linear combination of the input relations in their two-sided ideal, followed only by a nonzero scalar division over the coefficient field. A candidate is reduced against all currently committed rules before insertion.

Leading words therefore form an antichain under contiguous subword divisibility: an older leading word cannot divide a newly inserted one because of normal reduction; the new word cannot divide an older shorter one. Among equal lengths divisibility would require equality, also excluded by reduction. This is why separate inclusion ambiguities are unnecessary in this restricted degreewise algorithm. This justification would fail for a general nongraded completion.

For an overlap u=alpha*s, v=s*beta, the composition f*beta-alpha*g is formed with exact leading-coefficient cancellation. All proper nonempty suffix/prefix overlaps of eligible older rules are enumerated. A prefix hash index identifies candidates but full word equality is checked; hash collisions never decide algebraic equality. No queue of all future critical pairs is stored. At fixed d both parent degrees are below d, so newly inserted degree-d rules cannot create another degree-d proper overlap.

Disjoint replacements commute and need no critical pair. The only additional pair pruning implemented is the provably zero composition of two monomial zero rules. A term containing the leading word of a monomial zero rule is itself zero and can be deleted. We do NOT apply the commutative relatively-prime/product criterion to noncommutative words, discard arbitrary duplicate overlap words, or label this implementation F5.

## Reduction and arithmetic

Words use four bits per generator and two uint64 words. A length-20 word requires 80 significant bits, while its stored representation is 16 bytes. Its length is supplied by the homogeneous polynomial degree. A term occupies 24 bytes including its tagged coefficient.

The general normal form uses fraction-free pseudo-reduction: cancel a coefficient c by multiplying the current polynomial by the reducer's leading coefficient and subtracting c times the contextualized reducer, then divide primitive content. Sorted rows are merged, not expanded into Lisp trees. Two bounded scratch arenas alternate; cached reducers never point into the arena being overwritten.

The monic small-integer fast path uses a sparse hash accumulator plus a max-heap of reducible words. It processes the row in descending word order. Already extracted irreducible words cannot be generated by a later, smaller leading word. The original row is preserved until the entire fast reduction succeeds. Any non-unit pivot, coefficient overflow, large tagged coefficient, or insufficient table space abandons this optimization and returns to exact fraction-free reduction. A full table can retry with a larger bounded table. This is sparse polynomial reduction, not a batched F4 matrix algorithm.

Diagnostic `reductions` can include work from abandoned fast-path trials and scratch-replay attempts. It is not the number of distinct algebraic compositions.

## Parallel ownership

There is one shared WebAssembly.Memory and one coordinator plus 1..32 reduction workers. Each worker has a separate 128-KiB WASM call stack, private scratch partitions, and bounded read caches. There is no private copy of the full basis per worker.

All WASM instances must be instantiated before gn_init; otherwise module data initialization could reset shared state. Workers read an immutable snapshot. The coordinator submits at most one pending composition per active lane, joins ALL workers, and only then modifies basis metadata. Each worker result is reduced AGAIN against the now-current basis before committing. Commit order is deterministic by lane. Worker count can change tails/insertion history, so bytewise output equality is not a general correctness criterion.

On scratch exhaustion the coordinator can reduce the active lane count, repartition the SAME scratch pool, and replay the current degree. Previously committed valid rules are preserved. With one remaining lane, a row too large for the configured workspace produces SCRATCH_BUDGET rather than allocating without limit. This version does NOT implement out-of-core reduction of a single arbitrarily large working row.

## Memory and disk

The hard linear-memory ceiling is 15,000,000,000 decimal bytes, rounded down to a WASM 64-KiB page boundary (14,999,945,216 bytes). The wasm32 build is additionally capped at 4 GiB minus one page. The default host budget is much smaller; raising the maximum does not allocate all pages immediately.

The linear budget includes static state, reserved WASM stacks, fixed total scratch, bounded polynomial/divisor caches, resident leading-word/prefix metadata, and resident basis records when spill=false. C has no malloc, garbage collector, ECL runtime, or MEMFS. Persistent allocation is monotone and checked before growth. Host memory.grow exceptions become allocation failure. There is no hidden second linear heap.

With spill=true, immutable basis polynomial records are appended to OPFS. Leading words, record offsets, degrees, and overlap indexes stay resident. Old reducers are NOT deleted merely because their degree is smaller: they can still be necessary to reduce words of degree 20. Full reducer records are read through bounded per-lane caches and I/O buffers. Keeping only leading words on disk would not suffice to compute exact normal forms.

Metadata itself remains in RAM and can eventually exhaust the budget. A large individual row can exceed scratch capacity even with ample disk. These conditions cause a controlled stop; this backend does not promise every degree-20 presentation can finish inside 15 GB. Increasing worker count does not increase scratch: it decreases each lane's share and can hurt performance.

The hard budget is NOT a guarantee against OS/process OOM. Browser/JIT/JS heaps, worker overhead, virtual-memory reservation, disk quota, other tabs, and the operating system are outside the kernel allocator. Tests at 128 MiB do not establish that a 15-GB allocation succeeds on an arbitrary machine. A process may be killed externally before the allocator can report an error.

The JS host never creates a Uint8Array spanning a 15-GB buffer. It uses bounded offset views. Each OPFS lane uses a reusable 64-KiB non-shared transfer buffer, avoiding reliance on shared-buffer acceptance by FileSystemSyncAccessHandle. Text export is streamed in roughly 32-KiB chunks; UI preview is capped at 256 KiB by default and never exposes a half-polynomial. Very large coefficients (>131072 bits) are refused by the TEXT formatter; the exact binary basis and completed-degree checkpoint remain available. Thus even successful algebraic completion can report a subsequent export error instead of a text result.

## Checkpoints and interruption

OPFS layout: george-native/<runKey>/basis.gnb, checkpoint-0.json, checkpoint-1.json, result.gb. Record headers contain a magic, byte size, term count, homogeneous degree, and FNV-1a-style 64-bit corruption checksum. Large-coefficient offsets are relative to a record, allowing transfer between wasm32, wasm64, and native representations. This checksum detects many corruptions; it is NOT an algebraic certificate or a cryptographic integrity proof.

On completion of a degree, the basis is flushed first, then one of two alternating JSON checkpoint slots is written. The manifest records the SHA-256 identity of variables, relations, field, order, ABI, plus rule count, completed degree and exact binary prefix size. On resume, records are checked and re-indexed, and any unfinished suffix is truncated. Changing target upward is allowed; changing the presentation or field is not. A failed current degree is repeated from the last completed checkpoint.

An ordinary exclusive sync handle on coordinator.lock prevents cooperating coordinators/tabs from opening the same run concurrently. With OPFS's readwrite-unsafe handles on the basis file, the application provides coordination: only the coordinator appends, and a barrier separates worker reads from commits. Actual browser OPFS behavior and quota recovery are NOT end-to-end certified in the supplied test environment. Node tests emulate storage with fs but execute real shared-memory WASM workers.

Cancellation uses an atomic flag inspected inside reductions and pair enumeration. The George overlay asks workers to stop before delayed forced termination. Abrupt browser/tab/process termination can lose the current degree, not a previously flushed valid checkpoint (subject to storage failure). Keep external copies of important checkpoints; OPFS is origin-local and site-data clearing removes it.

## Remaining engineering work

A real browser + deployed George end-to-end test, browser-memory/RSS profiling at large allocations, disk quota fault injection, independently reproduced degree-10+ bases, broader randomized arithmetic testing, and sustained degree-20 runs remain necessary before treating this as a production scientific backend. Signatures, chain criteria, coefficient modular reconstruction, disk-resident overlap indexes, a true LRU reducer cache, and out-of-core active rows are not implemented. The current cache is bounded and simple rather than a sophisticated storage scheduler.
